section_summary: This section opens with postwar FBI and State Department correspondence concerning Nobuo Yatoh’s address book, possible Japanese contacts in Lima, and a request from São Paulo for American occupation films and photographs to counter Japanese messaging. Most of the section is the opening of the FBI’s secret November 1945 monograph The Japanese in Latin America, including its introduction, contents, illustrations, a historical and political survey of Japan, and the beginning of its analysis of organized Japanese migration. The monograph connects migration, centrally controlled colonies, trade, propaganda, nationalism, and intelligence activity throughout Latin America.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding information on Nobuo Yatoh’s Latin American contacts
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Hoover forwards a confidential memorandum identifying two people listed in Japanese agent Nobuo Yatoh’s address book.
subfiles.summary: Hoover recalls that examination of Nobuo Yatoh’s effects uncovered an address book containing possible contacts in several Latin American countries. He sends a Lima source’s identifications but emphasizes that neither identified individual was shown to have participated in Japanese affairs or espionage. Copies were provided to naval and military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning Nobuo Yatoh, Yoshio Ishii and Mario Aiki
subfiles.from: Confidential sources in Lima and a United States government official
subfiles.about: The memorandum identifies Yoshio or Yuzo Ishii and Mario Aiki as possible entries in Yatoh’s address book and reports the results of inquiries into them.
subfiles.summary: Japanese residents in Peru identified Ishii as a prosperous businessman, former Central American industrialist and former manager of a Lima toy store later operated by Seijiro Tabata. Another source reported that Ishii had been deported from Peru to the United States aboard the SS Frederick C. Johnson on January 10, 1943. A United States official stated that Mexico City photographer Mario Aiki had not recently been active in Japanese affairs and that espionage inquiries concerning him were negative.

subfiles.title: São Paulo telegram requesting American occupation films and photographs
subfiles.doc_type: incoming telegram with record-copy notice and duplicate
subfiles.from: United States mission in São Paulo; sender not named
subfiles.about: The telegram urgently requests films and photographs of the American occupation for public exhibition after receipt of a Japanese version of the emperor’s proclamation.
subfiles.summary: São Paulo reports receiving the Japanese version of the emperor’s proclamation and refers to an earlier telegram of May 6. It renews an urgent request for motion-picture shorts showing the American occupation and for photographs suitable for reproduction and public display. The following pages contain an administrative record-copy notice and a duplicate information copy of the same telegram.

subfiles.title: The Japanese in Latin America
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation, United States Department of Justice
subfiles.about: The opening portion of an FBI monograph surveys Japan’s development and the organization, scale and strategic implications of Japanese migration to Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The introduction argues that Japanese colonies in Latin America were fostered through subsidized shipping, businesses, diplomatic representation, organizations, schools and religious loyalties, creating communities closely tied to Japan. Contents, illustration lists, maps and statistical charts outline country studies of social, political, commercial, propagandistic and espionage activity across Latin America. Chapter 1 presents Japan’s geography, population, culture, religion, economy and political evolution, emphasizing nationalism, imperial ideology and military rule. Chapter 2 begins a history of emigration and describes government-directed selection, training, transportation and settlement of migrants, immigration restrictions, trade expansion and the early Japanese colonies in Brazil and Peru.
